abstract.p: The jute hairy caterpillar, Spilosoma obliqua (Lepidoptera: Erebidae) is considered as one of the major threats to jute cultivation. The best eco-friendly methods to combat these jute pests involve administration of nano-biopesticides, as a successful alternative to the toxic chemicals. In this study, a nano-biopesticide formulation containing green synthesized silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) using Ocimum sanctum leaf extract has been proposed. The characterization studies confirmed significant interactions between the Ag NPs and bioactive components in the nano-biopesticide formulation. The comparative analysis of the aforementioned larval mortality showed better responses in the nano-biopesticide formulation rather than the crude (pure) leaf extract. The LC50 values were calculated both for the nano-biopesticide formulation and pure extract after 24, 48 and 72 h of treatment. The nano-biopesticide formulation was found to exhibit the lowest and much promising LC50 value of 93.21 ppm, 23.38 ppm, 5.96 ppm relative to that of LC50 values of 1590.74 ppm, 459.30 ppm, 102.68 ppm respectively for the crude leaf extract. The synergistic interactions between the components in the nano-biopesticide formulation can be associated with its greater effectiveness as a promising toxicant to the larvae of the jute caterpillar compared to the mere leaf extract, thereby, demonstrating a greener and safer method for effective pest management.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Jute (Corchorus sp.), “The golden fiber of India”, is regarded as the major cash crop cultivated in Eastern India1. It satisfies all the standards for ‘safe’ packaging as it is a natural, recyclable, biodegradable, and environmental-friendly fibre product2. Indian jute industry manufactures varieties of usable and convenient jute products such as hessian or burlap (plain-woven fabrics), sacks (loosely woven cloth), food-grade jute cloths, yarns, carpet backing cloths, blankets, decorative fabrics, floor coverings, and shopping bags, etc. India ranks first in the global jute production and accounts for about 62.2% of world jute manufacture3. Around 9.98 million of jute bales are produced annually on 0.71 million hectares of land in India. West Bengal is one of the leading jute producer states in India4.

Jute is basically a summer crop (pre-kharif to kharif seasons). Its cultivation is often threatened by a range of insect pests such as jute hairy caterpillar (Spilosoma obliqua), yellow mite (Polyphagotarsonemus latus Banks), grey weevil (Myllocerus discolour Bohemus), stem weevil (Apion corchori Marshall), and jute semilooper (Anomis sabulifera Guen.)1. Due to such several insect infestations, jute output in India including West Bengal suffers a considerable economic loss of 31–34%1,5. Accordingly, for effective pest control and management, commercial chemical pesticides are being widely deployed. However, such traditional chemical pesticides, although effective for pests, create as well as cause serious environmental and health risks to all. To illustrate, the damage caused is because of two primary reasons: (a) the high toxicity and non-biodegradable nature of the chemicals, and (b) the residues in soil, water and crops adversely affects the environment6.

Plant-based biopesticides, in comparison, are safe to the environment, especially for humans and non-target organisms7–9. Several plant-based biopesticides like neemazal and chlorpyriphos, etc. have been successfully commercialized in the recent past10. Thus, the usage of natural plant based biopesticides offers an innovative, eco-friendly approach to pest control. Nonetheless, development of a plant-based biopesticide is a quite lengthy process seeking interdisciplinary expertise in extraction, isolation, separation, purification, structural elucidation, bioassay, regulatory and other related aspects. Further, supplements such as suitable stabilizing agents, UV-screening agents and antioxidants may often be required to enhance the stability, shelf life, bio-efficacy and to suppress the process of resistance development in the attacking insects. The cost and large-scale production of such substances are still questionable in view of wide commercial applications11. Nevertheless, one such promising source of plant based biopesticide is Ocimum sanctum (commonly known as holy basil or tulsi), known for its potent antimicrobial and insecticidal properties. Extracts from O. sanctum contain many useful and bioactive compounds such as eugenol, ursolic acid, and rosmarinic acid, etc12,13. Considerable number of reports are available employing the O. sanctum leaf extracts, comprising of bioactive allelochemicals, to control different agricultural pests thereby leading to the development of novel botanical insecticide(s) in the recent years14. Nonetheless, the mortality rates of the insects on deployment of mere phytochemicals are often found to be moderate and their applications become challenging particularly when large jute production economy is concerned10,15.

In the recent past, with the advent of nanoscience and nanotechnology, a revolution in the management of pests in agriculture has emerged. The beneficial outcomes of engineered nanomaterials as an active ingredient for the nano-formulations in insect pest control and plant protection have been extensively explored16,17. Nano-pesticides, compared to conventional chemical pesticides, have shown better eco-friendly characteristics. A great advantage of their small scale diminishes the non-specific actions on beneficial insects and microorganisms, which augments the protective outcome on crops. In addition, nano-scale usages of pesticides also provide better chances of reducing the risk of bulk contamination of the soil and water bodies18. Nanopesticides also render other benefits, which includes enhanced foliar adhesion, improved crop yield and quality in many cases19. These benefits, if harnessed appropriately, can promote higher crop yields and thus contributing towards sustainable agriculture, much needed in countries like India where agriculture is the main occupation of its major population.

Several bottom-up synthesis strategies involving physical, chemical and biological procedures for synthesis of nanomaterials with different shapes and morphology has been adopted20. Even though chemical methods are prompt and productive in a shorter amount of time21, nonetheless, most of the prevailing techniques use powerful, hazardous reducing agents which produces toxic waste and by-products, and often the derived nano-form is unstable in the biological environment with less fruitful targeted action22. As a result, a synthetic method for creating nanoparticles that is safe for the environment and does not require the use of hazardous chemicals or their by-products is currently mandated. These engineered compounds would exhibit enhanced bioavailability and desired targeted action against pests.

Among the various types of nanomaterials available till date, the metallic nanoparticles are more popular for their antimicrobial efficacy23. Different metal nanoparticles such as silver, gold, platinum, cobalt, nickel, copper, etc. have significant biocidal properties which have been exploited in designing proficient nano-biopesticides. Studies reveal that silver nanoparticles have the most unique insecticidal properties amongst the diverse class of metallic nanoparticles and thus, widely explored systems due to their facile synthesis and unique optical, electrical, and biological characteristics24,25. Further to add, the beneficial impacts of Ag nanoparticles as nano-fertilizer have also been detected over the last few years26,27. In many plants, it not only enhances the seed germination and plant growth, but also improves the quantum efficiency of the photosynthetic process, thus playing a crucial role in agriculture for ensuring sustenance security and improvement in crop production28. As far as its insecticidal activity is concerned, a recent study has been revealed that the Ag nanoparticles was successful in the infringement of the larval digestive system and caused their mortality, as the dead larvae showed indications of oozing of inner gut contents29.

Thus, the current focus is to implement appropriate procedure of green synthesis of silver nanoparticles to introduce readily available, cost-effective, eco-friendly and non-toxic biological agents to serve as both reductants as well as a stabilizing agent for the synthesized nanomaterials as well as reinforce the insecticidal activity of the resultant formulation Various phytochemicals such as phenolic compounds, alkaloids, terpenoids, sugars, and proteins serve as reductant cum stabilizing agents for the as-synthesized metal nanomaterials30–32. There are numerous illustrations of synthesis of silver nanoparticles from varied plant sources, such as Chrysanthemum morifolium33, Cassia auriculata34, Cinnamon zeylanicum35, and so on36.

Utilization of O. sanctum leaf aqueous extract, a simple, quick and easy as well as inexpensive method of synthesizing silver nanoparticles was deployed in the current work. Literature survey unveils that, eugenol, a major, volatile and pivotal organic compound found in the O. sanctum leaves, is a kind of phenylpropanoid chemical that is employed in insect traps to attract insects37,38. Thus, the synthesized bio-encapsulated silver nanoparticles (nano-biopesticide formulation) can now suitably and actively penetrate the pest’s cuticle more efficiently, ensuring higher mortality rates besides reducing the overall dosage of the bioactive agent needed. Moreover, such nano-biopesticide formulations will also check the chances of pest resistance, offer prolonged action, and assist in decreasing the environmental footprint associated with synthetic pesticides.

Therefore, the aim of the present study is to compare the effectiveness of O. sanctum-based nano-biopesticide formulation against S. obliqua with respect to the neat aqueous O. sanctum leaf extract39. As both the Tulsi leaf extract and the silver nanoparticles have insecticidal properties, a synergism in insecticidal action by the nano-biopesticide formulation is expected on optimizing the composition. The study also provides a fair scope to investigate the importance of the nanocomposite in promoting nano-bio-pesticidal activity and also offers a promising future for sustainable pest control in jute cultivation40.

sec.title: Reagents and chemicals
sec.p: Silver Nitrate (AgNO3) (ACS reagent, 99.0%), used in the synthesis of Nano-biopesticide formulation has been procured from Sigma-Aldrich. Besides, the other chemicals used in the study process such as Sulphuric Acid (H2SO4), Sodium Chloride (NaCl), Calcium Chloride (CaCl2), Acetone (C3H6O) have been obtained from Sisco Research Laboratory (SRL). Methanol (CH3OH) has been purchased from Rankem.

sec.title: Collection and identification of plant
sec.p: The leaves of O. sanctum were collected from Crop Research & Seed Multiplication Farm, The University of Burdwan, Golapbag, Bardhhaman, West Bengal, India having latitude of 23.250006° and longitude of 87.842667° respectively (as shown in the photograph of Fig. S1) (See Supporting Information file). The plant Ocimum sanctum was identified by Dr. Saikat Naskar, Assistant Professor and a voucher specimen no. BURD/12278/a, b & c/2024 was kept at the Department of Botany, The University of Burdwan.

sec.title: Preparation of Ocimum sanctum leaves extract
sec.p: Disease-free and fresh O. sanctum leaves were collected from the above-mentioned Crop Research & Multiplication Farm from the University of Burdwan, and subsequently washed for many times with distilled water to remove the dust particles. Then the leaves were air dried 24 h (one day) at room temperature (28 ± 2 °C). After air-dry, 30 g of the fresh, washed leaves were taken, sliced into small pieces and placed in a 1000 ml glass beaker along with 500 ml double distilled water. The combination was boiled in 30–40 min as the colour of the aqueous mixture is turned into greenish yellow. After boiling, the resultant extract solution was cooled to room temperature (28 ± 2°) and filtrated through Whatman filter paper No. 1. Then the leaf extract was stored at 4 °C for further use, as indicated in the photograph of Fig. S2 (See Supporting Information file).

sec.title: Synthesis of nano-biopesticide formulation
sec.p: At first, 1 M AgNO3 solution containing silver nitrate (0.169 g) (Sigma-Aldrich) was prepared using double distilled water (1000 ml). Now, the above prepared Ocimum sanctum leaf extract (10 ml) was added drop-wise to a given volume (80 ml) of 1 M AgNO3 aqueous solution with continuous stirring followed by mild heating at around 50–60 °C for 10–15 min, to ensure reduction of Ag+ ions to Ag nanoparticles (AgNPs). The resultant solution was then transferred to an incubator at 25 °C for 24 h. The solution gradually changed colour from yellowish to brown which indicated the formation of silver nanoparticles, well consistent with the earlier reports41. The entire procedure was conducted under a dark condition.

sec.title: Preparation of crude leaf product extract for comparative study
sec.p: Fresh O. sanctum leaves were obtained from Crop Research & Multiplication Farm at The University of Burdwan (latitude was 23.250006° and longitude was 87.842667°) and these fresh leaves were washed thoroughly with distilled water and placed in shaded condition (28 ± 2°) for a period of one week for drying. After air-dry, an electrical blender was used to pulverize the plant leaves. For the leaf extract preparation, 200 g of the above dry powdered substance was taken in a 1000 ml conical flask and impregnated with 500 ml methanol for 48 h and then filtered. The methanol extract of O. sanctum leaves crude or pure extract was concentrated at 40–50 °C by using hot air oven (HOA-1090 A).

A part of plant residue (1 g) was dissipated in acetone (100 ml) was recognized as 1% stock solution. From this stock solution, different specific concentrations were prepared ranging from 50, 200, 350, 500, 650 ppm respectively. (Indicated in the photographs demonstrated in the Fig. S3, See Supporting Information file)

sec.title: Analysis of stability of biosynthesized of nano-biopesticide formulation
sec.p: The stability of silver nanoparticles was accomplished against pH, and two types of salts solutions of sodium chloride and calcium chloride, were added to the synthesized nano-biopesticide formulation aqueous solutions for making 0.25 M, 0.025 M, 0.0025 M, and 0.00025 M concentration respectively in order to check the stability against salt stress conditions. Different pH conditions such as pH 1, pH 3, pH 5 and pH 10, were also prepared to study the stability of nano-biopesticide formulation. All the samples under the different stress conditions were analysed by using UV-Visible Absorption Spectroscopy (U-2900 Spectrophotometer, HITACHI, Japan).

sec.title: Larva collection
sec.p: Spilosoma obliqua larvae were collected from the Bijoypur, West Bengal 700121, India which Latitude 22.76482° and Longitude 88.435428° as illustrated in Fig. 1 and supplementary images in Fig. S4 (See Supporting Information file), and cultured in the laboratory by feeding with fresh jute leaves and maintained at 28 ± 1 °C. The different stages of the S. obliqua have been demonstrated in the Fig. S5 (see Supporting Information).

sec.title: Measurement of larval mortality
sec.p: We have employed five concentrations for treatment study and each concentration has 4 replications and for each case, 20 larvae were exposed for the larval mortality study. The lethal concentration (LC50) for the nano-biopesticide formulation was determined using a series of dilutions that ranged from 10 ppm, 20 ppm, 50 ppm, 100 ppm and 150 ppm (parts per million) (As indicated in the photograph in the Fig. S3, See Supporting Information file). The control leaves were treated with distilled water alone. After collecting the required number of larvae from the field and putting them in sterile, air-dried petri-dishes, jute leaves were coated with various concentrations of nano-biopesticide formulation and allowed to air dry. Larvae were fed with different concentrations of nano-biopesticide formulation treated jute plant leaves and controls were fed in water treated leaves. The uneaten plant leaves were taken out and replaced with fresh, treated and untreated ones in every 24 h. We regularly noted total number of larvae which was dead in all different concentrations. Similarly, in case of crude tulsi leaf extract, the concentrations were 50, 200, 350, 500 and 650 ppm and other procedure was similar to Ag NPs. To determine mean lethal concentrations (LC50), probit analysis was applied to the percent mortality data following corrections42. Mortality rates (MR) on groups of 20 S. obliqua larvae were measured (Fig. S6) (See Supporting Information file). sec.title: Characterization of the nano-biopesticide formulation
sec.p: The resultant green synthesized nano-biopesticide formulation was subjected to different characterization techniques such as UV-Visible Spectroscopy, Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), X-Ray Powder Diffraction (XRD), Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FE-SEM), Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS), Zeta potential and Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), Energy-Dispersive X-Ray (EDX) including elemental mapping were adopted to study in detail the morphology as well as the physicochemical properties so as to realize its effective role in the jute larval mortality.

sec.title: UV-visible spectrophotometry
sec.p: The absorption spectra of the crude leaf extract and the nano-biopesticide formulation were monitored by using ultraviolet-visible spectrophotometer (U-2900 Spectrophotometer, HITACHI, Japan) in the range of 200–700 nm.

sec.title: Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy
sec.p: To determine the nature of functional groups and moieties present in the samples, their FTIR spectra were studied. Dried samples were homogeneously blended with potassium bromide (KBr) and measured using FTIR Spectrometer (JASCO FT/IR: Model 4700) in the range of 4000–400 cm−1 range.

sec.title: Field emission scanning electron microscopy
sec.p: Morphology and size of synthesized silver nanoparticles in the resultant nano-biopesticide formulation were identified by using Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscope (FE-SEM, MODEL: SIGMA 300). Fiji software was used to analyse the nanoparticles size obtained from the SEM images.

sec.title: Transmission electron microscopy
sec.p: The samples morphology was also investigated in details using TEM analysis (JEOL; JEM 1400). The as-prepared samples were suspended in acetone and accordingly dropped on carbon-coated copper grids for TEM analysis.

sec.title: Dynamic light scattering for particle size measurement and zeta potential analysis
sec.p: Dynamic light scattering (DLS) which is based on the laser diffraction method with multiple scattering techniques was employed to study the average particle size of AgNPs in the resultant nano-biopesticide formulation. The prepared samples will be dispersed in de-ionised water followed by ultra-sonication. Then solution will be filtered and centrifuged for 15 min at 25 °C with 5000 rpm and the supernatant will be collected. The supernatant will be diluted for 4–5 times and then the particle distribution in liquid will be studied. DLS and zeta potential measurements were performed using Zetasizer Nano ZS (Malvern, UK) at a scattering angle of 90° using He-Ne Laser (λ = 632.8 nm).

sec.title: X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) analysis
sec.p: X-ray powder diffraction (MODEL: BRUKER D8 ADVANCE) with a CuKα radiation (λ = 0.15418 nm) was used for the phase identification of the finely ground, homogenized, synthesized material so as to obtain information on the crystalline phases present in the samples.

sec.title: Energy-dispersive X-Ray (EDX) and elemental mapping
sec.p: For EDX analysis, a small quantity of the sample was pasted on a carbon tape and coated with gold. The analysis was done using the instrument SEM (ZEISS EVO LS 10). Elemental signals and mapping for oxygen, nitrogen, carbon and silver were observed.

sec.title: Characterization of green synthesized silver nanoparticles from Ocimum sanctum (nano-biopesticide formulation)
sec.p: Physiochemical as well as morphological characterization of the nano-biopesticide formation and the leaf extract were evaluated by using popular techniques like UV-visible absorption spectroscopy, Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), Zeta potential study and particle size analysis, X-Ray Diffraction (XRD), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), and Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), Energy-Dispersive X-Ray (EDX) respectively.

The visible confirmation of the nano-biopesticide formulation was observed on gradual addition of silver nitrate solution (colourless) to the aqueous O. sanctum leaf extract (green-yellow) with constant stirring and mild heating, which immediately initiated the formation of silver nanoparticles, indicated by the visible colour transformation from yellow green to dark brown colour of the reaction mixture as depicted in the snapshot of Fig. 243. After 24 h, the colour of the reaction mixture further changed to dark brownish which represented complete bio-reduction of Ag+ ions to nano-sized silver form44.

sec.p: This has been further supported by the UV-visible absorption studies. Thus, Fig. 3 shows the comparative UV-visible absorption spectra of the pure leaf extract and the nano-biopesticide formulations scanned in the wavelength range between 250 and 700 nm. The peaks in the region at 280 and 320 nm in the neat leaf extract is a clear indication of the presence of polyphenolics in the O. sanctum extract in agreement with the available literature45,46. Formation of the silver nanoparticles in the nano-biopesticide formulation was further affirmed by the characteristic surface plasmon band at 440 nm of silver nanoparticles47. Moreover, the shift of the peaks observed in the leaf extract has been attributed to the interaction of the Ag NPs with the active components of the leaf extract.

FTIR analysis (Fig. 4) of the nano-biopesticide formulation was performed to recognize the possible interactions between the functional groups of biomolecules present in O. sanctum leaf extract and the Ag NPs48. The characteristic bands were obtained for the neat O. sanctum leaf extract and nano-biopesticide formulation respectively as indicated in the Table 149. The comparative study of the samples’ spectra in Fig. 4, shows several overlapping peaks in the range of 2400 cm−1 to 1000 cm−1, confirming the existence of the O. sanctum extract in the nano-biopesticide formulation. The band at 3400 cm−1 corresponds to O–H stretching typically observed for the hydrogen bonded alcohols and phenols which is very much broadened nano-biopesticide formulation sample. Similarly, the peaks assigned around 1600 cm−1 corresponding to N-H bond primary amines also gets shifted. Such shifting of peaks has also been observed in the relative peak positions of C–O stretching of alcohols, carboxylic acids, ethers and esters observed in the range 1200–1000 cm−1 as well. These shifting correspond to the association of Ag NPs with the corresponding functional groups present in the leaf extract contained in the nano-biopesticide formulation which originates due to their strong interactions with the associated Ag NPs in the nano-biopesticide formulation50. Therefore, the studies confirm that synthesized nanoparticles were chemically surrounded by biomolecules in the resultant nano-biopesticide formulation having functional groups of that of alcohols, ketones, aldehydes, amines, and carboxylic acids and thus prevent their agglomeration, thereby stabilizing the nano-biopesticide formulation51.

sec.p: This fact is again supported by the comparative size distribution analysis of the O. sanctum leaf extract and the nano-biopesticide formulation. Figure 5a shows the average size distribution of the neat O. sanctum leaf extract to be around 283 nm implying that the biomolecules remain largely associated through intermolecular hydrogen-bonding and other supramolecular non-covalent interactions. However, in presence of the Ag NPs in the nano-biopesticide formulation, some of such interactions get modified as a result of which the average particle size decreases to around 86 nm as depicted in the Fig. 5b. Such improved size distribution in the latter is also expected to be responsible for increased bio-insecticidal activity of the nano-biopesticide formulation compared to the neat plant leaf extract. Further this observation is manifested from the zeta potential data that shows reduction and partial compensation of the surface charge on account of adherence of the Ag NPs on the surface of biomolecules associated with O. sanctum leaf extract in the nano-biopesticide formulation compared to the neat O. sanctum leaf extract as indicated in the Fig. 5c and d respectively52.

The XRD spectrum (Fig. 6) of the nano-biopesticide formulation shows a number of Bragg reflection peaks at 2θ values of 27.6°, 32.2°, 38.3°, 44.2°, 46.1°, 54.8°, 57.3°,64.2° which are indexed to (210), (122), (111), (200), (231), (142), (241), (220) planes of pure silver based on the face-centered cubic structure (JCPDS, file No. 04-0783) well in agreement with the available reports53,54. Thus, the x-ray diffraction study clearly indicates the crystalline nature of the Ag nanoparticles present in the nano-biopesticide formulation. The average grain size of the silver nanoparticles formed in the process was estimated from the Debye-Scherrer equation [d = 1.1λ/βcosθ] by determining the width of the highest intensity peak of 32.2° corresponding to (122) Bragg’s reflection plane, where d is the crystalline size, λ is the wavelength of X-ray, β is the full width at half maximum of the diffraction peak and θ is the Bragg’s angle55. The average crystallite size of the obtained Ag nanoparticles was estimated to be around 43.11 nm from the FWHM of the (122) reflection.

To further study the morphology of the resultant nano-biopesticide formulation, TEM and SEM of the sample were explored. Figure 7a, b shows the TEM images of the silver nanoparticles present in the nano-biopesticide formulation. The morphology of the Ag nanoparticles appears to be spherical. It is also evident from the images that the silver nanoparticles are being surrounded by a faint thin layer of capping materials derived from O. sanctum leaf extract. The median size distribution of the nanoparticles stands around 20 nm with few particles seems to be agglomerated. It may be noted that the size of the silver nanoparticle obtained from TEM is in fair agreement with the crystallite size obtained from the XRD measurements. Further, Fig. 7c shows the scanning electron micrograph (SEM) of the bio-pesticide formulation indicating fair distribution of silver nanoparticles in the sample. The surface morphology of the nanoparticles is found to be relatively smooth and uniform. Figure 7d shows the average size distribution of the Ag NPs is around 18 nm which is in fair agreement with that of the TEM data. This particle size range also received support from the appearance of UV-vis absorption band at 440 nm56. It is obvious that some nanoparticles sizes are larger as the smaller Ag nanoparticles have strong tendency to agglomerate owing to their high surface energy and high surface tension. In addition, Energy Dispersive X-ray (EDX) was also conducted for the nano-biopesticide formulation to establish the existence of elemental silver and homogenous distribution of silver nanoparticles in the bioactive matrix as indicated in the Fig. 8a–f. The EDX spectrum (Fig. 8a) reveals the purity and the complete chemical composition of the sample. A noticeable percentage of silver metal is found to co-exist with other chemical elements. The reduced silver nanoparticles exhibited a characteristic peak at around 3 keV, well in agreement with other available reports57. Thus, the study revealed presence of metallic silver in the resultant nano-biopesticide formulation. The EDX analysis also provided the information about the presence of other elements such as Nitrogen (N), Oxygen (O), Carbon (C) apart from Silver (Ag) as depicted by the bar graph shown in the Fig. 8b. The existence of C, N, O elements along with Ag indicates the association of the biomolecules serving as capping organic agents bound to the surface of the silver nanoparticles and thus stabilizing the formulation, supporting the results already revealed from the zeta potential studies. This is further supported by the elemental mapping images, as shown in the Fig. 8c–f, indicating clearly the homogeneous distribution of Ag NPs on the biomolecule matrix.

sec.title: Stability of the nano-biopesticide formulation
sec.p: Recently, a significant number of studies have indicated that environmental dominating factors, such as pH, ionic strength, or ion composition can significantly transform the stability and characteristics of AgNPs. For instance, Cupi et al. demonstrated significant behavioural as well as toxicity actions of AgNPs with pH58. Similarly, ionic strength of the medium also plays a vital role in the environmental fate and transformation of nanomaterials by influencing their physicochemical properties and thereby altering their toxicity59. Accordingly, the stability of the nano-biopesticide formulation were explored through UV-visible absorption studies conducted with the sample under different pH conditions as it considerably relates to biological and therapeutic impact as well. As the medium pH was decreased from 10 to 1, the surface plasmon peak due to Ag NPs in the nano-biopesticide formulation gets significantly red shifted as well as broadened, suggesting augmentation in the hydrodynamic size of the nano-moiety as well as removal of the same from the colloidal state as indicated by the decreasing absorbance values in the Fig. 9a. From the negative zeta potential value of the biopesticide formulation as observed in Fig. 5d, it is obvious that increasing the acidity of the medium will neutralize the surface charge and accelerate the agglomeration of Ag NPs in the nano-biopesticide formulation. In addition, pH changes often affect the interparticle distances and dielectric constants of the medium which may also lead to aggregation process60. Thus, lowering of pH resulted in considerable broadening due to increase in polydispersity as well as suppression of the defined surface plasmon peak of the Ag NPs, signifying the increasing destabilisation and aggregation of nanoparticles in the nano-biopesticide formulation sample with increasing acidity.

Further, to study the influence of ionic strength on the stability of the nano-biopesticide formulation, UV-visible absorption studies were conducted with the sample under different NaCl concentrations as depicted in the Fig. 9b. Thus, NaCl concentrations were varied in between 0.00025 M, 0.0025 M, 0.025 M and 0.25 M and the changes in the absorption bands were accordingly monitored. Studies revealed that the rate of destabilization was very slow in NaCl, the absorbance value decreased to 77.5% on moving from 0.00025 M to 0.25 M NaCl concentration. Additionally, greater extent of peak broadening was also observed on increasing the ionic strength of the medium as the AgNPs underwent aggregation due to unfavourable salinity conditions. For advanced exploration studies on the role of ionic strength, the stability of nano-biopesticide formulation were now subjected to different concentrations of CaCl2 and monitored under UV-visible spectroscopy. The findings, as depicted in the Fig. 9c, suggest that as CaCl2 provides greater ionic strength than equimolar NaCl, as a consequence of which the rate of aggregation of the Ag NPs were much more prompt, as indicated by the rapid fall in absorbance to 55.3% as well as bands broadening observed on increasing the concentration from 0.00025 M, 0.0025 M, 0.025 M and 0.25 MCaCl2, thereby demonstrating significant loss in the stability of the dispersion. Thus, the study also confirms that the higher positive charge of the ions also readily induces the loss of the stability of the Ag NPs in the nano-biopesticide formulation61.

For comparison, the absorption studies of the neat O. sanctum leaf extract were also conducted. The pH variation, as observed in Fig. 10a, showed broadening as well as increase of the absorption with increasing pH which may be due to increase in solubility of the polyphenolic compounds present in the O. sanctum leaf extract. Studies of ionic strength shows by varying the concentration of NaCl from 0.00025 M to 0.25 M has negligible impact on the absorbance of the O. sanctum leaf extract as observed in Fig. 10b. However, the absorbance values were significantly affected and rather non-monotonous in behaviour with the varying the concentration of CaCl2 from 0.00025 M to 0.25 M for the O. sanctum leaf extract. It therefore appears that the solubility of the active chromophore components in the O. sanctum leaf extract increases on increasing the concentration of CaCl2 from 0.00025 to 0.0025 M and then starts decreasing with further increasing in ionic strength of CaCl2 from 0.0025 to 0.25 M.

sec.title: Comparison of the efficacy between the nano-biopesticide formulation and pure Ocimum sanctum extract against Spilosoma obliqua
sec.p: Nanotechnology provides a big scope of substituting toxic synthetic chemical pesticides in controlling the agricultural insect pests. Several reports conformed the effectiveness of management of various insect pests and plant diseases using biosynthesized nanomaterials62. For instance, biosynthesized AgNPs have demonstrated larvicidal toxicity against Culex quinquefasciatus, Aedes aegypti, and Anopheles stephensi in the recent past62. Furthermore, green copper nanoparticles demonstrated remarkable outcomes when tested against Aedes aegypti, Culex quinquefasciatus, and Anopheles stephensi utilizing LC50 and LC90 measurements63. In another study, silver nano treatment was effective against high insecticidal activity of Tinea pellionella (L.) larvae64. Similarly, Murugan et al. reported that AgNPs made from C. scalpelliformis and C. agardh killed 80% of Cx. quinquefasciatus larvae in their first to fourth instars at low concentrations65. In our study, the efficacy of nano-biopesticide formulation and the pure O. sanctum extract at different concentrations were tested against Jute hairy caterpillar (S. obliqua). Considerable mortality was evident from the studies of the treatment of nano-biopesticide formulation on the above-mentioned pest. It has been observed that concentration plays important role in larvicidal activity. As the concentration and time increases, mortality also increased which is depicted in Fig. 11. The different concentrations of nano-biopesticide formulation and crude extract were employed for the studies were 10 ppm, 20 ppm, 50 ppm, 100 ppm, 150 ppm and 50 ppm, 200 ppm, 350 ppm, 500 ppm, 650 ppm (parts per million) respectively. Both experiments were conducted for the duration of 24, 48 and 72 h. In these two experiments, nano-biopesticide formulation gave the percentage of mortality at 24 h in 10 ppm concentration was 10%. Similarly, the mortality in 20 ppm, 50 ppm, 100 ppm and 150 ppm concentrations were 25%, 35%, 45% and 65%. In 48 h, the nano-biopesticide formulation displayed % of mortality of 30%, 50%, 65%, 75% and 90% in 10 ppm, 20 ppm, 50 ppm, 100 ppm and 150 ppm concentrations respectively. At 72 h, the percentage of mortality for nano-biopesticide formulation at 10 ppm, 20 ppm, 50 ppm, 100 ppm, 150 ppm concentrations were 65%, 80%, 90%, 95%, 100% respectively which has been highlighted in Table 2. As the concentration and days after treatments were increased, the larval mortality of 2nd instar larva S. obliqua also got improved. Thus, the results of larvicidal activity clearly indicate that the percentage of mortality is directly proportional to the concentration of the nano-biopesticide formulation solution. Accordingly, the nano-biopesticide formulation have shown higher efficacy than the original leaf extract. In case of pure leaf extract, the percentage of mortality which was depicting in Table 2 is low rather than nano-biopesticide formulation. Crude/ pure extract from O. sanctum gave the mortality at 24 h in 5%, 15%, 20%, 25%, 40% at 50 ppm, 200 ppm, 350 ppm, 500 ppm, 650 ppm concentration respectively. Similarly, in same concentration, percentage of mortality in 48 and 72 h for the original leaf extract were 15%, 40%, 45%, 50%, 55% and 35%, 65%, 75%, 75%, 75%, respectively. We have also evaluated the LC50 value which is defined as the concentration of a substance that is lethal to 50% of the organisms in a toxicity test. As a general rule, the longer the exposure, the lower the LC50 value. The lower value of LC50 signifies greater toxicity towards the pest. Probit analyses have shown variations in virulence. In our experiments, the LC50 values of nano-biopesticide formulation at 24, 48 and 72 h were 93.21 ppm, 23.38 ppm and 5.96 ppm respectively. In case of pure leaf extract, the LC50 values were 1590.74 ppm, 459.30 ppm, 102.68 ppm at 24, 48 and 72 h correspondingly which was depicting in Table 3. In nano-biopesticide formulation, which were produced from O. sanctum gave the lowest LC50 values 5.96 ppm against 2nd instar larva of S. obliqua after 72 h exposure while in case of pure leaf extract the lowest LC50 value after 72 h was around 102.68 ppm. All probit and LC50 analysis have been depicted in Fig. 12. In comparing LC50 values, a lower LC50 indicates higher toxicity because it means a smaller amount of the substance is required to cause harm to 50% of the test organisms. So, in our experimental view, after 72 h, the LC50 value of the Ag NPs based nano-biopesticide formulation was 5.96 ppm indicating higher toxicity for the assigned pest to greater effectiveness at lower concentrations compare to that of the pure leaf extract having LC50 value of 102.68 ppm after 72 h under identical experimental conditions. Thus, the present study explores the facile synthesis and application of silver nanoparticles-based nano-biopesticide to ensure effective management of jute pests. The combination of O. sanctum extract with potent antimicrobial and insecticidal properties, together with silver nanoparticles in the nano-biopesticide formulation exhibited enhanced physicochemical stability and broad-spectrum activity, thereby representing a promising approach for sustainable agriculture, particularly for pest management in jute (Corchorus capsularis). Our experimental findings demonstrate significant efficacy of the nano-biopesticide formulation against key jute pests such as the jute hairy caterpillar (S. obliqua). The mode of action appears to be twofold. Several bioactive components in the O. sanctum such as Eugenol have been reported to disrupt the pests’ cell membranes and respiratory enzymes, leading to the insect mortality. The silver nanoparticles too have lethal action on the pest and their combinations have significantly and synergistically enhanced the pesticidal effect. The synergistic effect observed between bio-active components of O. sanctum such as eugenol (found as major component) and Ag nanoparticles in nano-biopesticide formulation can be attributed to their complementary mechanisms to disrupt cellular functions and generate reactive oxygen species (ROS), resulting in a more potent and durable pesticide effect than either components alone. Additionally, the silver nanoparticles provide a controlled-release mechanism for eugenol, thereby enhancing its persistence on jute plants and reducing the frequency of application66.

sec.title: Conclusion, challenges and future prospects
sec.p: The results of this study confirm that the nano-biopesticide formulation comprising of the Ocimum sanctum extract based silver nanoparticles represent a potent, eco-friendly, and sustainable alternative to conventional pesticides for jute pest management. The synergy between various bioactive components in the O. sanctum extracts and Ag NPs effectively mitigate pest infestations while minimizing environmental impact.
Despite the promising results, several challenges need to be addressed before large-scale application of O. sanctum extract based silver nanopesticides in jute cultivation:

list-item.p: Although the synthesis of silver nanoparticles is more cost-effective than in the past, the integration of O. sanctum extract in nano-biopesticide formulations may still present economic constraints for the resource-limited farmers.

While the laboratory results are promising, the stability and performance of nano-biopesticide formulation comprising of green synthesized AgNPs from O. sanctum under varying field environmental conditions (such as rainfall, soil pH, and UV exposure) need further investigation.

The introduction of nano-biopesticides into the market requires thorough evaluation by regulatory authorities. The safety profile of silver nanoparticles, especially concerning soil health, beneficial organisms, and possible human exposure, needs to be rigorously studied to ensure compliance with environmental safety standards.

sec.p: Although challenges remain, particularly regarding cost and regulatory concerns, the integration of green synthesized AgNPs from O. sanctum into jute farming practices holds significant promise for reducing dependence on chemical pesticides in the near future, promoting sustainable crop protection, and safe guarding environmental and human health.

Thus, the current investigation has well established the effectiveness of the green, semi synthetic Ag NPs -Ocimum sanctum-based nano-biopesticide formulation as a promising insecticide in eradicating the major pest (jute hairy caterpillar, S. obliqua) in jute crops.
